title: Cross-paradigm breach pattern: Centralized identity custodian failures
description: Major breaches of centralized identity systems — India's Aadhaar biometric database leaks (2017-2018), the U.S. OPM breach (2015, 21.5M records), Estonia's ID card cryptographic vulnerability (2017) — demonstrate that centralized custodians concentrate vulnerability. Each breach exploited the gap between the system's technical capacity to aggregate data and the institution's actual capacity to secure it.
source: Documented security incidents in national and enterprise identity systems (NIST, Krebs on Security, academic post-mortems)

title: Federated and decentralized systems shift but preserve the vulnerability surface
description: OAuth/SAML federation moved the trust problem to identity providers and token exchange boundaries (e.g., the 2020 SolarWinds SAML golden ticket attack on federated enterprise identity). Decentralized identity (SSI/DID) pushed custody to wallet software and key management, where usability studies show ordinary users routinely fail to protect private keys, and wallet provider compromises re-centralize risk at the software layer.
source: SolarWinds CISA advisory (2020); Whitten & Tygar 'Why Johnny Can't Encrypt' lineage of usability research; W3C DID Working Group implementation reports

title: Limits of formal verification in closing institutional gaps
description: Formally verified cryptographic protocols (e.g., the verified TLS implementation miTLS, sel4 microkernel) achieve mathematical guarantees within their model boundaries, but verified systems still depend on unverified institutional processes: key ceremony governance, update deployment policy, legal compliance, and human operational procedures. The gap between model and deployment is itself an instance of the accountability gap.
source: Bhargavan et al. (2017) miTLS verification; Klein et al. (2009) seL4 verification; Bellovin 'Thinking Security' (2015) on the model-reality gap

title: Statistical pattern of governance failure following technical confidence
description: Empirical studies of organizational security posture (e.g., Ponemon Institute annual reports, Verizon DBIR) consistently find that organizations with the highest technical security investments still suffer breaches attributable to institutional factors: misconfigured access controls, insider threats, delayed patching due to organizational inertia, and regulatory non-compliance. The correlation between technical investment and breach prevention plateaus — suggesting a structural floor set by institutional, not technical, constraints.
source: Verizon Data Breach Investigations Reports (2015-2024); Ponemon Institute 'Cost of a Data Breach' longitudinal studies
